root.note: Proto-Germanic *blankaz. Borrowed into Late Latin as blancus.

history: Latin had its own word for white, albus. Portuguese uses a Germanic one. The Germanic peoples who ruled Iberia and Gaul after Rome, Visigoths, Suebi and Franks, had *blank, ‘shining, bright’, and it spread into Late Latin as blancus. Portuguese then did what it often does with l after a consonant and turned it into r: blanco became branco, just as Latin placere became prazer, ‘pleasure’. Albus did not vanish. It survives in alvo, which once meant ‘white’ and today means ‘target’, and in alvorada, ‘dawn’. English blank is a cousin of branco: a blank page is a white page. A glass of white wine in Portugal is um copo de vinho branco.
historyEinfach: Branco means ‘white’. The word is not Latin. It comes from the Germanic peoples who lived in Iberia after the Romans. Their word was blank, ‘shining’. Portuguese changed bl into br. English blank, like a blank page, comes from the same word.

elsewhere.text: English got blank back from French: a blank page is a white page.
The old Latin white lost the colour job but kept work in other Portuguese words.
